title: The Power of a Knight on H7! | King’s Indian Defense | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: White opens with the knight to f3; we reply with the knight to f6.
White claims space with c4.
We start the fianchetto with g6.
White builds the big centre with d4.
We complete the fianchetto with the bishop to g7.
White chooses g3 — the Fianchetto Variation, one of the most respected and positionally dangerous answers to the King's Indian.
We castle. We haven't committed to a King's Indian yet — that comes when we push ...d6.
White fianchettoes the bishop to g2.
We play d6, committing to a traditional King's Indian.
White develops the knight to c3 — a wide theoretical crossroads.
We choose the knight to d7, preparing a quick ...e5 — the most classic, King's-Indian-like setup.
White castles.
We strike in the centre with e5.
White's main try — striking back with e4, a Maroczy-like clamp with pawns on c4 and e4.
Rather than release with ...exd4, we play the older, trickier c6 — a line that slips past even experienced fianchetto players.
White plays h3.
We bring the queen out to a5 — the whole point of the line.
White plays the bishop to e3 — the modern top recommendation, where players used to prefer the rook to e1.

Against the older rook to e1, the idea is to release with ...exd4 just before White can push d5 and lock the centre — and then White must choose between the bishop and the routine knight recapture on d4.

The annoying reply is the bishop recapture on d4: then the natural ...Ne5 would run into c5, undermining the knight — and if we take on f3, the queen recaptures and our f6-knight suddenly hangs. That's why we keep the knight on d7 for now.
So we pick the low-hanging fruit — the rook to e8, a move that can't hurt us — and wait for White to show his cards.
White answers with the rook to e1.
We reroute the queen to c7, so that ...Ne5 finally becomes playable — the knight can't sit on d7 forever, blocking in the c8-bishop.

The point of ...Qa5: it can swing to h5, and it eyes the knight on c3 — so White can't slot in the useful b3 to defend c4, because b3 would simply drop that knight, a common blunder even at higher levels.
